A lot of people have real trouble thinking about the aggregate behavior of groups. They can only think about individuals.

So they think about Elon Musk as an individual. Maybe they think that he must be retarded, because they need that for emotional reasons. Or maybe they think he is a talented rocket designer.

But even if they realize he understands rockets, they can only think about him as an individual doing tasks. Not about his impact on what the whole company does.

If Elon Musk is just a talented rocket designer, then he can spend all day, every day, improving rocket designs.

But he is just one of 7000 engineers. So even if did a perfect job, he would only improve progress by about .014%

So, when a midwit looks at SpaceX, he sees 7000 engineers, and says to himself "Elon Musk cannot possibly be designing the whole damn rocket himself. These people are giving him too much credit."

This would be absolutely true if Musk were just a some random SpaceX engineer. But he isn't. He's the absolute dictator of the whole damn company.

He decides, with absolute and unquestionable authority, which behaviors are punished and which are rewarded.

Why is this important?

When I worked at Boeing, on various classified projects, I naively came in with the assumption that I was a software engineer, employed to design and build functional software as quickly and cheaply as possible.

Because of this, I focused on functionality and efficiency, for example suggesting changes that would obviate the need for entire projects and software components.

And I very rapidly became persona non grata.

At first, this caused me to adopt an air of aggrieved innocence. I was just trying to do my job well, and I was being punished for it.

Then I gradually came to realize that I hadn't properly understood what my job was, or what the actual mission of Boeing Defense, Space, and Security was.

Boeing DSS was not an aerospace company. Boeing DSS was a fraud company.

Its goal was twofold. First, to maximize transfer of public tax dollars to stockholder pockets. Second, to maintain the appearance of being an aerospace company, to prevent the fraud from being exposed.

Which meant that my real job was twofold. First, to generate billable hours. Second, to look busy.

This is why Space Launch System sucks. Why it is always late when it doesn't fail outright. Why it is at 300% of its target budget. Why it leaves American astronauts stranded and needing a lift from SpaceX.

That's because, for Boeing, building rockets is a side quest. Something they have to do to look busy. Yes, a rocket does occasionally fly, but that's just happening so programs don't get shut down.

For Boeing, coming in early and under budget would actually be failure. The system is functioning exactly as designed.

The cost, not the rocket, is the goal.

Musk and SpaceX don't work like that.

Unlike Boeing executives, Musk is not a useless grifter asshole. He is an entirely different kind of asshole... a rocket obsessed sperg.

So, at SpaceX, engineers do not get rewarded for generating billable hours. They get rewarded for making rockets fly. And for all the subtasks of this, like figuring out how to make rockets lighter, figuring out how to make engines reignite better, figuring out how to make rocket exhaust not destroy launch pads, etc.

And this attracts engineers who care about rockets. You've seen them on broadcasts, crying on open microphones because they dedicated their lives to something and it just flew.

As a rocket engineer, who designs rockets, Musk is probably replaceable. As a rocket company engineer, who designs rocket companies, he is not.

For over 50 years, the US space industry stagnated precisely for the lack of a Musk-like figure, who could not only create an effective aerospace company, but who could thereby demonstrate what an effective aerospace company looks like.

Which makes it much more difficult for fraudsters to get away with fraud.

I'm envious. I wish I could have worked for an aerospace company instead of a fraud company.

But what's more important is that some of us now no longer have to play "who gets the most cheese?".

They get to play "What can we build today?".

What was the significance of this weekend's SpaceX tower catch:

"Catching the second stage is substantially harder than catching the first stage because the Ship returns from orbit while the booster returns from a short suborbital hop. The booster separates minutes after liftoff, performs a brief boostback, and comes back from only a few hundred kilometers away at relatively low speed. Ship must reach orbital velocity, deploy payload, coast for many hours, execute a precise deorbit burn, survive full reentry heating, and only then perform its landing burn. As such, Ship must carry a functional heat shield, fly a long guided atmospheric trajectory from the other side of the planet, and execute a high-energy flip into the “chopsticks” while protecting its heat-shield side. Those combined demands of orbital energy, thermal protection, long-range guidance, and final precision are why a Ship catch is so incredibly difficult. No prior system, including the Space Shuttle, recovered a rocket-style orbital stage in this manner. The catch validates the path to full reusability which is the foundation of Starship’s cost and cadence targets. This is particularly important in driving the economics of orbital data centers." - DB

Morgan Stanley’s Adam Jonas on @SpaceX successfully catching Starship on flight 15:

“In our view, Flight 15 is a historic inflection moment for the company and spaceflight as a whole. SpaceX has recovered three Starship + many hundreds of Falcon 9 boosters in its history, and now others have accomplished the same. However, no entity has ever even attempted to recover a rocket upper stage in history (not counting Space Shuttle) given the intense thermal and mechanical stress of orbital re-entry.

With an upper stage now recovered intact, SpaceX can conduct a deep inspection of Ship 42 and use the findings to improve future vehicles in a way that was never previously possible. We believe it also helps clear the path to ramping full reuse of both booster and ship, the last major technical milestone before weekly or even daily Starship flights become realistic.

With a ship catch, SpaceX has materially de-risked the longer-term TAMs across all 3 of its segments.”

Yes, the green flame is caused by burning copper from depleting fuel in the regenerative cooling circuit and going oxygen-rich (closer to stoichiometric temperature) in the main combustion chamber.

Slight underperformance of engines on this flight is the reason. The booster is meant to land with tiny residuals, so the solution is to improve engine performance and performance consistency (underway with Raptor V3.2), as well as adjust flight software to do MECO1 about one second earlier to ensure enough propellant for boostback and landing (tiny change).

These early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand, so this booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights.
